newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia-Japan coal talks start next week.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia-Japan coal talks start next week.

text.p: Negotiations are due to start in Tokyo next week in the first round of the 1997/98 Australia-Japan coal pricing talks, the most important single determinant of annual traded coal prices in Asia and perhaps in the world.
Talks will be between Australia's biggest coal producer, the Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd (BHP), and the Japanese steel mills, a BHP spokesman told Reuters.

Australia, the world's largest exporter of coal, was recently forecast by the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics to export A$8.24 billion worth of coal in 1996/97, up from A$7.76 billion in 1995/96.
Japan is Australia's largest customer for coal, which is Australia's largest single export commodity.

Ian Dymock, public affairs manager for BHP Australia Coal, told Reuters that BHP will be negotiating for its wholly-owned mines and for its joint-venture partners in Central Queensland Coal Associates and in the Gregory mine in Queensland.
Asked if there was anything which he could say on the outlook for 1997/98 (April-March) coal pricing terms with Japan, Dymock said: "No".
"It would just be speculating at this stage," he said.
"Perhaps after the first round we will have some idea which way they're heading," he said.
"They'll lay their cards on the table and we'll lay our cards on the table and take it from there," he said.
"We'll probably have a reasonable understanding of which way they're heading, of whether they're going to be settled reasonably quickly or its going to be protracted," he said.

The opening of the first formal round of coal pricing talks follows an informal opening gambit by Australian producers in late October, after the annual Australia-Japan Business Co-operation Committee meetings in Sydney, for a price rise of more than 10 percent on hard coking coal.
Tight market supply of hard coking coal and a stronger Australian dollar were listed by Australian producers at the time.
Last year, Australia negotiated a price rise of of about five percent to about US$54.50 for hard coking coal in the 1996/97 Japanese fiscal year, which begins April 1.
A rise of slightly more than 10 percent for 1997/98, as informally requested by the Australians in October, would translate to a price rise of $6.00 a tonne.
